papers.title: Turnout: Adaptive Attention Switching for Efficient Reasoning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27500v1

summary.one_liner: Turnout converts a pretrained full-attention transformer into a hybrid that can switch each layer between full and fixed-size linear attention during reasoning, with the switching policy learned by reinforcement learning under a reward for correctness and memory use.
summary.plain: Large language models remember what they have written so far in a memory store that keeps growing as they generate longer answers. This paper takes an existing model and swaps part of that growing memory for a fixed-size one, which saves memory but tends to make reasoning answers less accurate. The authors' method lets the model decide, layer by layer and during generation, when to use the full memory and when to use the cheaper one.
summary.why: Long reasoning chains make memory use a practical bottleneck, so a way to trade memory for accuracy in a controlled way could matter for running such models on limited hardware. The text reports that the learned policy gives a better accuracy-versus-efficiency trade-off than fixed or static baselines, but it gives no specific numbers here, so the size of the gain is unclear.
summary.background:
- Transformer attention: the mechanism in language models that looks back at earlier tokens; full attention stores a key-value cache that grows with output length.
- Linearization: replacing that growing cache with a fixed-size state, which uses less memory but can lose information.
- Post-hoc distillation: training a new, cheaper component to imitate an already-trained model, without retraining from scratch.
- Hybrid model: a model that contains both full and linear attention paths and can use either.
- Reinforcement learning: training a decision policy by rewarding good outcomes; here the reward balances answer correctness against memory use.
- Pareto frontier: the set of options where you cannot improve accuracy without spending more memory, or vice versa.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc transformer linearization replaces the key-value cache of full attention, which grows linearly with generation length, with a fixed size state. This change reduces memory consumption but often hurts accuracy. In reasoning tasks, which require long generations, this effect is especially pronounced. In this work we introduce Turnout, a method that mitigates accuracy loss as a result of linearization, while maintaining its memory-reduction benefits. We apply post-hoc linearization to a pretrained full-attention model, training a linear path through distillation while leaving the original full-attention path unchanged. During response generation, the resulting hybrid model retains both paths and uses a learned policy to control when each layer switches from full to linear attention. We train the policy with reinforcement learning using a reward that balances answer correctness and memory use. Empirical evaluation of our method shows that the learned adaptive policy achieves a better accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier on reasoning tasks compared to fixed switching and static hybrid baselines.

papers.title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27973v1

summary.one_liner: MemOnce proposes a language model architecture that stores compact final-layer hidden states as memory, decodes them back into attention KV caches on demand, and uses sparse retrieval whose indices are computed once and shared across layers, aiming for linear-time cost in long, continual use.
summary.plain: Chatbots and other language models normally keep a large working notebook of everything said so far, and that notebook grows quickly as conversations get longer. This paper proposes a different way to keep that memory: it saves only a small, compressed version of the model's internal notes and rebuilds the detailed working notes when they are needed. The authors report that, when they adapted a 4-billion-parameter Qwen3.5 model this way, the stored memory shrank about 1313 times and prefill latency (the initial processing delay before a reply) dropped 6.9 times at a 1-million-token context.
summary.why: Memory growth is a practical bottleneck for models used over long, repeated sessions, so a way to cut it while keeping detail could matter for deployment costs. The reported figures come from the authors' own experiments, and the text does not show how the approach performs on tasks beyond those described, so its wider significance is still unclear.
summary.background:
- Transformer language models store a KV cache: per-token key and value vectors for each layer, used so the model can look back at earlier text.
- That cache grows linearly with context length in GPU memory, and attention compute grows quadratically with it.
- Linear-time alternatives compress history into a fixed-size state, which is cheap but can lose fine detail.
- Sparse attention means each new input attends only to a selected subset of past memory rather than everything.
- Prefill latency is the delay before the model produces its first output token, while it processes the input.
- Results are reported by the authors; the text gives no independent validation.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. In contrast, linear-time architectures compress history into fixed-size states, but struggle to retain fine-grained details. We introduce MemOnce, a foundation architecture that learns scalable memory states for language models. MemOnce is based on two core designs: (a) Memory encoder-decoder: it caches only a small subset of final-layer hidden states as compact memory representations and dynamically decodes them back into KV caches for attention layers; (b) Memory sparse attention: for each continual input, MemOnce adaptively retrieves relevant memory representations, with the sparse indices computed only once across layers. Coupling these two designs enables efficient on-the-fly memory loading and KV cache decoding, drastically reducing the GPU memory footprint and achieving linear-time complexity. We conduct extensive experiments to show that MemOnce outperforms Transformers and other architectures across varying model sizes, context lengths, and training paradigms (pretraining and post-training adaptation). In particular, adapting Qwen3.5-4B with MemOnce reduces memory state cache by 1313$\times$ and prefill latency by 6.9$\times$ at 1M context, and improves throughput by 3.5$\times$ and overall memory performance by +5.77%. Finally, MemOnce generalizes zero-shot to downstream representation tasks, achieving competitive results against specialized models.
